facts: Rice was not only food during the Sengoku period; it was a military supply that sustained prolonged warfare.
Control of highly productive land translated directly into economic, military and political power for regional rulers.
By the end of the period, land and harvest surveys increasingly expressed productive capacity in koku of rice and connected village output to taxation.
The rice-centred assessment of domains was formalised under the rulers who reunified Japan at the close of the Sengoku age.

sources.publisher: Cabinet Office, Government of Japan — Highlighting Japan

facts: Sengoku daimyō built fortified castles as military and administrative centres of their domains.
They drew their warrior retainers out of the countryside and into settlements around those castles, where they could serve in standing forces.
Around ninety new castle towns appeared between 1572 and 1590 alone.
Constructing and supplying these towns attracted labourers, artisans, merchants and service workers, turning military headquarters into urban economies.

sources.publisher: University of Colorado Boulder — Program for Teaching East Asia

facts: Political fragmentation and nearly continuous competition among regional lords disrupted older hierarchies during the Sengoku period.
The expression gekokujō, often rendered as ‘the lower overcoming the higher,’ describes the era’s reversals of rank and authority.
People of low status who demonstrated unusual ability in warfare or government could sometimes advance through a lord’s service.
Such advancement was possible but exceptional rather than a general disappearance of social rank.
Portuguese travellers introduced matchlock firearms to Japan on Tanegashima in 1543.
The island’s lord, Tanegashima Tokitaka, acquired two guns and directed local craftspeople to reproduce them.
Japanese workshops copied and manufactured the weapon rapidly; matchlocks consequently became known as tanegashima.
Their large-scale adoption made firearms an important factor in the battles of the later Warring States period.

facts: Toyotomi Hideyoshi rose from humble origins in Owari Province to become one of Japan’s three great unifiers.
After entering Oda Nobunaga’s service, Hideyoshi advanced through administrative and military assignments.
In 1573, meritorious service brought him three districts in northern Ōmi Province and the status of daimyō.
After Nobunaga’s death in 1582, Hideyoshi defeated Akechi Mitsuhide, succeeded to national leadership and continued the reunification of Japan.
